warmup.q: payment.status is AUTHORIZED. After val captured = payment.also { it.copy(status = Status.CAPTURED) }, what is captured.status?
options: It doesn't compile: the block of also must return Unit
It throws, because data classes are immutable
warmup.why: also runs the block and then returns the object it was called on. Its block has the type (T) -> Unit, so the copy the block makes is thrown away. Kotlin 2.4.21 compiles this without a warning. payment.let { it.copy(...) }, or simply payment.copy(...), gives you the copy.

sections.h: A scope function is a two-line function you could write yourself
sections.html:
Here is code that builds a gateway request and logs it. It is how most of us write it on day one:

Java
PaymentRequest request = new PaymentRequest();
request.setAmount(new Money(1_999, "EUR"));
request.setMerchantId("m-42");
request.setReference(order.id());
log.info("sending {}", request);
Kotlin
val request = PaymentRequest()
request.amount = Money(1_999, "EUR")
request.merchantId = "m-42"
request.reference = order.id
log.info("sending {}", request)

Nothing is wrong with it. It repeats request. on every line, and nothing marks where the setup ends. Kotlin code often says the same thing like this:

Java
// Java equivalent: a helper that takes a Consumer and returns the object
PaymentRequest request = apply(new PaymentRequest(), r -> {
    r.setAmount(new Money(1_999, "EUR"));
    r.setMerchantId("m-42");
    r.setReference(order.id());
});
log.info("sending {}", request);
Kotlin
val request = PaymentRequest().apply {
    amount = Money(1_999, "EUR")
    merchantId = "m-42"
    reference = order.id
}.also { log.info("sending {}", it) }

apply and also look like keywords. They are ordinary functions in the standard library, a couple of lines each. Here are let and apply written by hand:

Java
static <T, R> R let(T value, Function<T, R> block) { return block.apply(value); }
static <T> T apply(T value, Consumer<T> block) { block.accept(value); return value; }
Kotlin
fun <T, R> T.myLet(block: (T) -> R): R = block(this)                 // object in as `it`, block's result out
fun <T> T.myApply(block: T.() -> Unit): T { block(); return this }   // object is `this` inside, object out

Both are extension functions on any type T. The difference is the type of block. (T) -> R is a plain function type: the object arrives as the lambda's parameter, it. T.() -> Unit is a function type with a receiver, which "Function types, lambdas and closures" showed briefly: inside the lambda the object is this, so amount = ... means this.amount = .... Java has no lambdas with a receiver, which is why the Java helper needs r. on every line.

The real let in the Kotlin 2.4.21 standard library is that same line plus two things:

@kotlin.internal.InlineOnly
public inline fun <T, R> T.let(block: (T) -> R): R {
    contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) }
    return block(this)
}

inline makes the compiler paste the block into your code, so no lambda object exists at run time ("Higher-order functions: functions in, functions out" explained why). The contract is the next section's topic. So every scope function has one of these shapes, and the five differ in exactly two ways: whether the block sees the object as this or as it, and whether the call returns the object or the block's result.

try.title: One block, five functions, two answers
steps: Open ScopeReturns.kt. The same block, amountMinor * 2, runs through all five scope functions. Write down what each line prints before you run it.
Run it.
On the also line, change also to let. Predict the output, then run it.
Read ScopeReturnsJava.java: what does Java write for each one?

code.title: ScopeReturns.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06 data class Charge(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String) class ChargeRequest { var amountMinor: Long = 0 var currency: String = "" override fun toString() = "ChargeRequest($amountMinor $currency)" } // The two shapes, written by hand. A scope function is nothing more than this. fun <T, R> T.myLet(block: (T) -> R): R = block(this) // object as `it`, returns the block's result fun <T> T.myApply(block: T.() -> Unit): T { block(); return this } // object as `this`, returns the object fun main() { val charge = Charge("ch_1", 1_999, "EUR") // the same block, five ways: what comes back? println("let -> ${charge.let { it.amountMinor * 2 }}") println("run -> ${charge.run { amountMinor * 2 }}") println("with -> ${with(charge) { amountMinor * 2 }}") println("also -> ${charge.also { it.amountMinor * 2 }}") println("apply -> ${charge.apply { amountMinor * 2 }}") // the hand-written versions behave the same way println("myLet -> ${charge.myLet { it.amountMinor * 2 }}") println("myApply -> ${ChargeRequest().myApply { amountMinor = 1_999; currency = "EUR" }}") }

alt.title: ScopeReturnsJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java has no scope functions and no lambdas with a receiver. This is what each one stands in for, * plus the two shapes written as static methods. */ public class ScopeReturnsJava { record Charge(String id, long amountMinor, String currency) {} static class ChargeRequest { long amountMinor; String currency = ""; @Override public String toString() { return "ChargeRequest(" + amountMinor + " " + currency + ")"; } } // let: hand the value to a function, return what it returns static <T, R> R let(T value, Function<T, R> block) { return block.apply(value); } // apply/also: hand the value to a block, return the value itself static <T> T apply(T value, Consumer<T> block) { block.accept(value); return value; } public static void main(String[] args) { Charge charge = new Charge("ch_1", 1_999, "EUR"); // let, run and with all compute something from the object System.out.println("computed -> " + charge.amountMinor() * 2); // also and apply keep the object, whatever the block did System.out.println("kept -> " + charge); System.out.println("let -> " + let(charge, c -> c.amountMinor() * 2)); // no receiver: the block must name its parameter and write r. on every line System.out.println("apply -> " + apply(new ChargeRequest(), r -> { r.amountMinor = 1_999; r.currency = "EUR"; })); } }

try.expect: let, run and with print 3998, because they return the block's result. also and apply print the Charge itself: they run the block and drop its result. myLet and myApply behave the same, because that is all the real ones do. Changing also to let changes the value of the whole expression from the Charge to 3998. In Java, "compute something" is a plain expression and "keep the object" needs a helper that takes a Consumer.

sections.html:
Because the five differ in only two ways, two questions pick one.

First, what should the expression give back? If you want the same object (to keep chaining it, return it or assign it), use apply or also. If you want something new, a computed value or a different object, use let, run or with.

Second, how does the block use the object? If it mostly sets or calls the object's own members, a receiver reads best: apply, run, with. If it passes the object to other functions, or it also needs the this of the class around it, use an argument: also, let.

The figure puts the answers in a grid. The Kotlin docs give the same advice as a list of purposes, and each purpose lands in one cell:

You want to Use Payments example
configure an object apply PaymentRequest().apply { amount = total; merchantId = id }
do something extra and keep the object also authorize(req).also { audit.record(it) }
run code on a non-null value, or scope a temporary let card.token?.let { vault.lookup(it) }
configure and compute a result run client.run { timeoutMs = 800; charge(req) }
run statements where an expression is needed run { } val limit = run { val base = tier.limit(); base + overdraft }
group calls on an object you already have with with(settlement) { "$merchantId paid $amount on $date" }

run and with do the same job. with(x) { } reads well on a line of its own; x.run { } is the one that fits in a chain and after ?.. There is no ?.with.

The five share one more property, and it explains code that looks like it shouldn't compile:

Java
// Java equivalent: a lambda can't assign a local at all, so this is a plain statement
Authorization auth = gateway.authorize(request);
final String authCode = auth.code();
Kotlin
val authCode: String
val auth = gateway.authorize(request).also { authCode = it.code }   // compiles

A val may be assigned only once, and here the assignment sits inside a lambda. The compiler accepts it because also declares a contract, callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE): a promise that the block runs right here, exactly one time. All five scope functions declare it. Write your own also without the contract and the same line fails with Captured values cannot be initialized because of possible reassignments. Contracts are an Experimental API that the compiler trusts and never checks. The Advanced Kotlin track covers them in "Contracts and context parameters".

Because the five are inline, a bare return inside the block returns from the function around it, not from the block. In payment?.let { if (it.isTest) return; ledger.post(it) }, a test payment leaves the whole function.

Rows: the object is this, or the object is it. run and with: this, block result. apply: this, the object. let: it, block result. also: it, the object."><text class="t" x="300" y="40" text-anchor="middle">returns the block's result</text><text class="t" x="500" y="40" text-anchor="middle">returns the object itself</text><text class="t" x="100" y="106" text-anchor="middle">object is this</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="100" y="126" text-anchor="middle">(receiver)</text><text class="t" x="100" y="196" text-anchor="middle">object is it</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="100" y="216" text-anchor="middle">(argument)</text><rect class="box-a" x="210" y="70" width="180" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="300" y="100" text-anchor="middle">run, with</text><text class="t-s" x="300" y="124" text-anchor="middle">compute from members</text><rect class="box-b" x="410" y="70" width="180" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="500" y="100" text-anchor="middle">apply</text><text class="t-s" x="500" y="124" text-anchor="middle">configure an object</text><rect class="box-a" x="210" y="160" width="180" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="300" y="190" text-anchor="middle">let</text><text class="t-s" x="300" y="214" text-anchor="middle">transform, null check</text><rect class="box-b" x="410" y="160" width="180" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="500" y="190" text-anchor="middle">also</text><text class="t-s" x="500" y="214" text-anchor="middle">side effect, keep the value</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="320" y="262" text-anchor="middle">Non-extension run { } has no object: a block where an expression is needed.</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="320" y="284" text-anchor="middle">All five are inline and run the block exactly once, right there.</text></svg>

code.title: ValInit.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06 import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind import kotlin.contracts.contract data class Authorization(val code: String, val amountMinor: Long) fun authorize(amountMinor: Long) = Authorization("A-${amountMinor % 997}", amountMinor) // a hand-written also: not inline, no contract fun <T> T.plainAlso(block: (T) -> Unit): T { block(this); return this } // the same plus what the stdlib adds: inline and an EXACTLY_ONCE contract @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> T.contractAlso(block: (T) -> Unit): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } block(this) return this } fun main() { val code1: String val auth1 = authorize(1_999).also { code1 = it.code } // the stdlib's also: compiles println("also: $code1 for ${auth1.amountMinor}") val code2: String val auth2 = authorize(4_250).contractAlso { code2 = it.code } // yours, with the contract: compiles println("contractAlso: $code2 for ${auth2.amountMinor}") // Uncomment the next two lines and run again. The compiler can't know how often plainAlso calls the block. // val code3: String // authorize(700).plainAlso { code3 = it.code } }

alt.title: ValInitJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** Java equivalent: a Java lambda can't assign a local variable at all, so the assignment is a plain statement. */ public class ValInitJava { record Authorization(String code, long amountMinor) {} static Authorization authorize(long amountMinor) { return new Authorization("A-" + amountMinor % 997, amountMinor); } public static void main(String[] args) { final String code1; Authorization auth1 = authorize(1_999); code1 = auth1.code(); // a statement, outside any lambda System.out.println("statement: " + code1 + " for " + auth1.amountMinor()); // Uncomment the next two lines and run again. javac rejects any assignment to a local inside a lambda. // String code3; // Consumer<Authorization> keep = a -> code3 = a.code(); } }

try.expect: The first run prints also: A-5 for 1999 and contractAlso: A-262 for 4250. With plainAlso, the build fails with Captured values cannot be initialized because of possible reassignments., because the compiler can't see how often the block runs. Without the contract, inline is not enough: the errors are 'val' cannot be reassigned. and Variable 'code2' must be initialized. The contract is what carries the promise. javac says local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final: Java never lets a lambda assign a local.

sections.h: Four bugs that compile without a warning
sections.html:
Scope functions are inlined, so they cost nothing at run time. Their cost is in reading. Each of these four compiles on Kotlin 2.4.21 without a warning, and each one looks fine in a code review.

The first is ?.let { } ?: run { } used as if/else. Here it fronts a cache:

Java
String settle(Payment cached, Ledger ledger, Supplier<Payment> fetch) {
    return Optional.ofNullable(cached).map(ledger::post)   // map turns a null result into empty
            .orElseGet(() -> ledger.post(fetch.get()));
}
Kotlin
fun settle(cached: Payment?, ledger: Ledger, fetch: () -> Payment): String? =
    cached?.let { ledger.post(it) }          // post returns null for a duplicate
        ?: run { ledger.post(fetch()) }

It reads as "if cached, post it, else fetch and post". But ?: tests the value on its left, and that value is the result of the let block, not cached. ledger.post returns null for a payment it has already seen, so a cache hit on a duplicate runs both branches: one database fetch and a second post. Java's Optional.map(...).orElseGet(...) has exactly the same trap. Write the branch you mean with if or when, or decide the value first: val payment = cached ?: fetch(), then post once.

The second is also or apply used to compute. payment.also { it.copy(status = CAPTURED) } returns the original payment, because the block's type is (T) -> Unit and the copy is dropped. payments.apply { sumOf { it.amountMinor } } returns the list, not the total. A declared type catches the second one (val total: Long = ... fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Long', actual 'List<Payment>'.). Nothing catches the first. When you want the block's result, use let or run.

The third is nested receivers. In form.apply { fx.apply { amount = 500 } }, the bare amount binds to the innermost receiver that has one, fx. Delete amount from Fx a year later and the same line still compiles, and now it writes form.amount. A change in one class has changed code in another. Java's double-brace initialization follows the same rule and has the same trap. Don't nest apply; write the target (fx.amount = 500).

The fourth is a nested it. In merchants[id]?.let { schedules[it.scheduleId]?.let { "${it.name}: ${it.rateBps} bps" } }, the second it.name is the schedule's name, not the merchant's. Java can't make this mistake: it makes you name both lambda parameters and refuses to reuse a name. In Kotlin, name them, or better, flatten the chain:

Java
Merchant merchant = merchants.get(id);
if (merchant == null) return id + ": no fee schedule";
FeeSchedule schedule = schedules.get(merchant.scheduleId());
if (schedule == null) return id + ": no fee schedule";
return merchant.name() + ": " + schedule.rateBps() + " bps";
Kotlin
val merchant = merchants[id] ?: return "$id: no fee schedule"
val schedule = schedules[merchant.scheduleId] ?: return "$id: no fee schedule"
return "${merchant.name}: ${schedule.rateBps} bps"

steps: Read ScopeBugs.kt. For each of the four numbered parts, predict what it prints.
Run it.
In class Fx, delete var amount: Long = 0. In part 3, change the println to print only form.amount. Predict the value, then run.
Run ScopeBugsJava.java. Which of the four bugs does Java share, and which can't it have?

code.title: ScopeBugs.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06 enum class PayStatus { AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED } data class Pay(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long, val status: PayStatus) class MiniLedger { private val posted = mutableSetOf<String>() /** Returns a ledger entry id, or null when this payment was posted before. */ fun post(p: Pay): String? = if (posted.add(p.id)) "LE-${p.id}" else null } fun settleCached(cached: Pay?, ledger: MiniLedger, fetch: () -> Pay): String? = cached?.let { ledger.post(it) } ?: run { println(" cache miss, fetching from the database") ledger.post(fetch()) } class Fx { var amount: Long = 0 } class Form { var amount: Long = 0; val fx = Fx() } data class Shop(val name: String, val scheduleId: String) data class Schedule(val name: String, val rateBps: Int) fun main() { val p = Pay("p1", 1_999, PayStatus.AUTHORIZED) println("1. ?.let { } ?: run { }") val ledger = MiniLedger() println(" first settle: ${settleCached(p, ledger) { p }}") println(" second settle: ${settleCached(p, ledger) { p }}") println("2. also and apply drop the block's result") val captured = p.also { it.copy(status = PayStatus.CAPTURED) } println(" status after also { copy }: ${captured.status}") val total = listOf(p, p).apply { sumOf { it.amountMinor } } println(" total from apply { sumOf }: $total") println("3. nested apply") val form = Form().apply { fx.apply { amount = 500 } } println(" form.amount = ${form.amount}, form.fx.amount = ${form.fx.amount}") println("4. nested it") val shops = mapOf("m-1" to Shop("Acme Books", "eu-std")) val schedules = mapOf("eu-std" to Schedule("standard-eu", 290)) val label = shops["m-1"]?.let { schedules[it.scheduleId]?.let { "${it.name}: ${it.rateBps} bps" } } println(" label: $label") }

alt.title: ScopeBugsJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Optional; import java.util.Set; import java.util.function.Supplier; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** The same four bugs, as close as Java gets. Two of them exist in Java too; one Java's compiler prevents. */ public class ScopeBugsJava { enum Status { AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED } record Pay(String id, long amountMinor, Status status) { Pay withStatus(Status s) { return new Pay(id, amountMinor, s); } } static class MiniLedger { private final Set<String> posted = new HashSet<>(); /** Returns a ledger entry id, or null when this payment was posted before. */ String post(Pay p) { return posted.add(p.id()) ? "LE-" + p.id() : null; } } static String settleCached(Pay cached, MiniLedger ledger, Supplier<Pay> fetch) { // Optional.map turns a null result into empty, so orElseGet runs: the same trap as ?.let ?: run return Optional.ofNullable(cached).map(ledger::post).orElseGet(() -> { System.out.println(" cache miss, fetching from the database"); return ledger.post(fetch.get()); }); } static class Fx { long amount; } static class Form { long amount; Fx fx = new Fx(); } record Shop(String name, String scheduleId) {} record Schedule(String name, int rateBps) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Pay p = new Pay("p1", 1_999, Status.AUTHORIZED); System.out.println("1. Optional.map(...).orElseGet(...)"); MiniLedger ledger = new MiniLedger(); System.out.println(" first settle: " + settleCached(p, ledger, () -> p)); System.out.println(" second settle: " + settleCached(p, ledger, () -> p)); System.out.println("2. peek drops the block's result, like also"); Pay captured = Stream.of(p).peek(x -> x.withStatus(Status.CAPTURED)).findFirst().orElseThrow(); System.out.println(" status after peek { withStatus }: " + captured.status()); System.out.println("3. double-brace initialization, Java's nested apply"); Form form = new Form() {{ fx = new Fx() {{ amount = 500; }}; }}; System.out.println(" form.amount = " + form.amount + ", form.fx.amount = " + form.fx.amount); System.out.println("4. Java makes you name both lambda parameters, and refuses to reuse a name"); Map<String, Shop> shops = Map.of("m-1", new Shop("Acme Books", "eu-std")); Map<String, Schedule> schedules = Map.of("eu-std", new Schedule("standard-eu", 290)); String label = Optional.ofNullable(shops.get("m-1")) .flatMap(shop -> Optional.ofNullable(schedules.get(shop.scheduleId())) .map(schedule -> shop.name() + ": " + schedule.rateBps() + " bps")) .orElse(null); System.out.println(" label: " + label); } }

try.expect: The second settle prints cache miss, fetching from the database and then null, although the payment was in the cache: the let block returned null, so run ran too. also { copy } leaves the status AUTHORIZED, and apply { sumOf } prints the list. The nested apply gives form.amount = 0, form.fx.amount = 500; after you delete Fx.amount, the unchanged line sets form.amount = 500 and the compiler says nothing. The label is standard-eu: 290 bps, the schedule's name. Java shares the first three (orElseGet, peek, double-brace initialization) and gets the label right, because both parameters have names.

sections.h: Nulls are values: ?., ?:, takeIf and requireNotNull
sections.html:
A Java developer new to Kotlin often reaches for Optional. You don't need it. A nullable type T? is not a wrapper. In the words of the Kotlin docs, "at runtime, objects of nullable types and objects of non-nullable types are treated the same": the checks all happen at compile time. The operators do what Optional's methods do, with no extra object:

Java Optional Kotlin
opt.map(f) x?.let(f) or x?.f()
opt.orElse(d) x ?: d
opt.orElseGet(() -> ...) x ?: run { ... }, also lazy
opt.orElseThrow() x ?: throw ... or requireNotNull(x)
opt.filter(p) x?.takeIf(p)
opt.ifPresent(c) x?.let(c) or x?.also(c)

The right side of ?: can return or throw, because both are expressions in Kotlin. That turns a guard clause into one line, and every line after it works with a non-null value:

Java
String token = card == null ? null : card.token();
if (token == null) return new Declined("no card token");
Kotlin
val token = card?.token ?: return Declined("no card token")

takeIf { } is a filter for one value: the object if the predicate holds, null if not. It earns its place inside a chain, as in amount.takeIf { it > 0 }?.let(::charge). As a guard on its own, a plain if reads better. The predicate always runs, so keep side effects out of it. For collections, mapNotNull { } maps and drops the nulls in one pass.

When a null means somebody broke a rule, fail loudly and say why. requireNotNull(x) { "..." } throws IllegalArgumentException, for bad input from a caller. checkNotNull(x) { "..." } throws IllegalStateException, for our own broken state. Both carry a contract that tells the compiler x is not null afterwards, so x is smart-cast from the next line on. !! throws a NullPointerException with no message at all. Java's Objects.requireNonNull(x, "...") takes a message but still throws NullPointerException.

Smart casts have one limit you will hit. A var property is never smart-cast, because other code could change it between the check and the use. if (pendingRefund != null) send(pendingRefund) fails with Smart cast to 'Long' is impossible, because 'pendingRefund' is a mutable property that could be mutated concurrently. This is where ?.let is the right tool: pendingRefund?.let(send) reads the property once. val refund = pendingRefund ?: return works too.

Arrow, the library in the next lesson, gives the same advice about its own Option type: "Typically, when working in Kotlin, you should prefer working with nullable types over Option as it is more idiomatic." It keeps Option for nested nullability in generic code and for libraries such as Reactor that forbid null.

try.title: Four null tools, two languages
steps: Run NullTools.kt, then NullToolsJava.java. Compare the exception each null check throws.
In Checkout.process, uncomment the if line and run. Read the error, then comment it out again.

code.title: NullTools.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l06 data class CardOnFile(val token: String?, val country: String) data class RefundLine(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long?, val reason: String?) class Checkout { var pendingRefund: Long? = null fun process(send: (Long) -> Unit) { // Uncomment the next line and run: a var property is never smart-cast, even right after the check. // if (pendingRefund != null) send(pendingRefund) pendingRefund?.let(send) // reads the property once, then works with that value } } fun tokenFor(card: CardOnFile?): String { val token = card?.token ?: return "declined: no card token" // ?. chains, ?: can return return "charge with ${token.take(4)}..." } fun main() { println(tokenFor(CardOnFile("tok_4242424242", "NL"))) println(tokenFor(CardOnFile(null, "NL"))) println(tokenFor(null)) // takeIf: a filter for one value; the result is nullable val amount = 1_999L println("takeIf positive: ${amount.takeIf { it > 0 }}, takeIf over 5,000: ${amount.takeIf { it > 5_000 }}") // requireNotNull and checkNotNull: a message, the right exception, and a smart cast afterwards val line = RefundLine("p9", null, "duplicate") try { val cents = requireNotNull(line.amountMinor) { "refund ${line.paymentId} has no amount" } println(cents) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("requireNotNull: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } val ledgerSession: String? = null try { checkNotNull(ledgerSession) { "ledger session not opened" } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("checkNotNull: ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } // mapNotNull: transform and drop the nulls in one step val lines = listOf(line, RefundLine("p10", 500, null), RefundLine("p11", 1_200, "fraud")) println("reasons: ${lines.mapNotNull { it.reason }}") val checkout = Checkout().apply { pendingRefund = 700 } checkout.process { println("sending refund of $it") } }

alt.title: NullToolsJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l06; import java.util.List; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.Optional; /** The same null handling with Optional and Objects. Note which exception each check throws. */ public class NullToolsJava { record CardOnFile(String token, String country) {} record RefundLine(String paymentId, Long amountMinor, String reason) {} static String tokenFor(CardOnFile card) { Optional<String> token = Optional.ofNullable(card).map(CardOnFile::token); if (token.isEmpty()) return "declined: no card token"; return "charge with " + token.get().substring(0, 4) + "..."; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(tokenFor(new CardOnFile("tok_4242424242", "NL"))); System.out.println(tokenFor(new CardOnFile(null, "NL"))); System.out.println(tokenFor(null)); // Optional.filter is the closest thing to takeIf long amount = 1_999L; System.out.println("filter positive: " + Optional.of(amount).filter(a -> a > 0).orElse(null) + ", filter over 5,000: " + Optional.of(amount).filter(a -> a > 5_000).orElse(null)); // Objects.requireNonNull throws NullPointerException; Kotlin's requireNotNull throws IllegalArgumentException RefundLine line = new RefundLine("p9", null, "duplicate"); try { Objects.requireNonNull(line.amountMinor(), "refund " + line.paymentId() + " has no amount"); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("requireNonNull: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } // mapNotNull: map, then drop the nulls List<RefundLine> lines = List.of(line, new RefundLine("p10", 500L, null), new RefundLine("p11", 1_200L, "fraud")); System.out.println("reasons: " + lines.stream().map(RefundLine::reason).filter(Objects::nonNull).toList()); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints IllegalArgumentException: refund p9 has no amount and IllegalStateException: ledger session not opened; Java's Objects.requireNonNull prints NullPointerException: refund p9 has no amount. The if line fails with the smart-cast error, because pendingRefund is a var property. With requireNotNull, the second call stops main with an IllegalArgumentException. That is worse here: a card without a token is an expected outcome (a decline), not a bug, so it belongs in the return value. The next lesson makes that line its whole topic.

sections.h: A checklist you can run in five seconds
sections.html:
When your fingers are about to type a scope function, run down this list and stop at the first line that settles it.

  1. Do you need one at all? A plain call, a?.b(), an if on a local val, or val x = y ?: return is often clearer. Detekt ships UnnecessaryLet and UnnecessaryApply rules for exactly this case.
  2. What should the expression give back? The same object: apply or also. Something new: let, run or with.
  3. How does the block use the object? Its own members: apply, run, with. Passed to other functions, or the outer this must stay visible: also, let.
  4. Is the value nullable? Use ?.let, ?.run, ?.also or ?.apply, never with. If you add ?: something, make sure the block on the left can never produce null. If it can, write if or when.
  5. Is the block nested, longer than about five lines, or the third link in a chain? Extract a function or use named vals. The Kotlin docs ask you not to nest scope functions, because "it's easy to get confused about the current context object and value of this or it".

Try the list on one line: PaymentRequest().apply { reference = order.id }.also { log.info("sending {}", it) }. Line 1 has something to say about the apply: a block with a single assignment is exactly what detekt's UnnecessaryApply flags. Line 2 approves of the also: it is a side step, and the request flows on unchanged.

analogy: Think of a post office counter. You hand over a parcel. With apply, the clerk works on the parcel itself, adds stamps and a label, and hands the same parcel back. With also, the clerk photographs it for the records and hands it back untouched. With let or run, the clerk weighs it and hands you a receipt with the price: you get something new back, and the parcel drops out of the conversation. this or it is whether the clerk opens the parcel and works inside it, or treats it as one item to pass along. The analogy breaks in one place: a real clerk who promised you a receipt can't secretly repackage your parcel too. A run block can change the object and return something else, and none of the five stops you from doing the wrong kind of work inside the block.
world: Scope functions show up all over a Quarkus payments service. ProducerRecord(topic, key, value).apply { headers().add("idempotency-key", key.toByteArray()) } configures a Kafka record before send. .also { meter.counter("payments.sent").increment() } counts it without touching it. Panache entities are where the null rules bite: their fields are var properties, so entity.cardToken is never smart-cast, and entity.cardToken?.let { vault.lookup(it) } or a local val is the right tool. And look hard at every ?.let { ... } ?: run { ... } around a repository or a map lookup. HashMap.put returns the previous value, which is null the first time, so found?.let { cache.put(id, it) } ?: run { log.warn("missing") } warns on every first insert.
mistake: The most common real mistake is reading x?.let { A } ?: run { B } as "if x, then A, else B". People write it because it looks like Optional.map(...).orElseGet(...) or Swift's if let, and in the happy path it behaves that way. But ?: checks the value of the whole left side, which is the result of block A. Whenever A ends in a call that can return null (a repository find, map[key], HashMap.put, a save() that returns an optional id), B runs as well, after A already did its work. In payments that means a second fetch, a second post or a misleading log line. The fix is to write the branch you mean: if (x != null) A else B, or a when. If A is only a side effect, x?.also { A } ?: B is safe, because also returns x itself, which is not null.

compare.title: Configure, log and compute: scope functions vs plain Java

java.title: Checkout.java
java.html: PaymentRequest request = new PaymentRequest(); // configure: a variable and setters request.setAmount(order.total()); request.setMerchantId(order.merchantId()); request.setReference(order.id()); log.info("sending {}", request); // a side step is just a statement long risk = riskModel.score(request.getAmount(), request.getMerchantId()); // compute String token = Optional.ofNullable(card).map(Card::token) // null check with a message .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("no card token"));

kotlin.title: Checkout.kt
kotlin.html: val request = PaymentRequest().apply { // configure: this, returns the request amount = order.total merchantId = order.merchantId reference = order.id }.also { log.info("sending {}", it) } // side step: it, returns the request val risk = request.run { riskModel.score(amount, merchantId) } // compute: this, returns the score val token = requireNotNull(card?.token) { "no card token" } // null check with a message

compare.note: At run time the two are the same. Every scope function is inlined, so the bytecode is the same local variable, setter calls and statements the Java version has. What differs is what the code tells the reader and what the compiler can check. apply puts the whole setup in one block, so the request is finished when the block ends, and also marks the log line as a side step that can't change the value flowing through. Java needs an Optional object to chain a null check; Kotlin's ?. and requireNotNull exist only at compile time, and requireNotNull smart-casts what follows. Java lambdas have no receiver and can't assign locals. That is why Java has no apply and no val-inside-also, and also why it can't have the nested-receiver bug.

steps.say: A refund handler written as one expression. gateway.refund returns null when the acquirer rejects the refund. Before reading on, find every outcome that ends up in the wrong place.
steps.code: fun handleRefund(cmd: RefundCommand): RefundOutcome = payments.find(cmd.paymentId)?.let { it.takeIf { it.status == Status.CAPTURED }?.let { gateway.refund(it.id, cmd.amount) }?.let { RefundOutcome.Accepted(it) } } ?: run { RefundOutcome.NotRefundable(cmd.paymentId) }

alt.html: RefundOutcome handleRefund(RefundCommand cmd) { return payments.find(cmd.paymentId()) // Optional<Payment> .filter(p -> p.status() == Status.CAPTURED) .map(p -> gateway.refund(p.id(), cmd.amount())) // null when rejected: map makes it empty .<RefundOutcome>map(RefundOutcome.Accepted::new) .orElseGet(() -> new RefundOutcome.NotRefundable(cmd.paymentId())); }

steps.say: Three different failures come out as one. A payment that doesn't exist, a payment that isn't captured, and a refund the acquirer rejected all become null somewhere in the chain, so ?: run reports all three as NotRefundable. Support will tell the merchant to stop retrying a refund that only failed at the acquirer. And there are four its with three meanings.

Rewrite it top to bottom. 1. Load, and leave early if it's missing. 2. Check the business rule. 3. Do the work, and name its failure. 4. Put the happy path last. Each failure now has its own outcome, and no line depends on which it is in scope.
steps.code: fun handleRefund(cmd: RefundCommand): RefundOutcome { val payment = payments.find(cmd.paymentId) // 1. load ?: return RefundOutcome.NotFound(cmd.paymentId) if (payment.status != Status.CAPTURED) // 2. check the rule return RefundOutcome.NotRefundable(payment.id, payment.status) val refundId = gateway.refund(payment.id, cmd.amount) // 3. act ?: return RefundOutcome.Rejected(payment.id) return RefundOutcome.Accepted(refundId) // 4. the happy path, last }

alt.html: RefundOutcome handleRefund(RefundCommand cmd) { Payment payment = payments.find(cmd.paymentId()).orElse(null); // 1. load if (payment == null) return new RefundOutcome.NotFound(cmd.paymentId()); if (payment.status() != Status.CAPTURED) // 2. check the rule return new RefundOutcome.NotRefundable(payment.id(), payment.status()); RefundId refundId = gateway.refund(payment.id(), cmd.amount()); // 3. act if (refundId == null) return new RefundOutcome.Rejected(payment.id()); return new RefundOutcome.Accepted(refundId); // 4. the happy path, last }

steps.say: A scope function still has a place here: a side step that must not change the result. also logs the outcome and returns it unchanged, which is what the reader expects from the word.
steps.code: return RefundOutcome.Accepted(refundId) .also { log.info("refund accepted: {}", it) } // side step: the value flows through

alt.html: RefundOutcome outcome = new RefundOutcome.Accepted(refundId); log.info("refund accepted: {}", outcome); // Java: just a statement return outcome;

lab.title: Fix four scope-function bugs at the settlement desk
steps: Run the tests. Four of ten fail, one for each function in SettlementDesk.kt. Read each failure message before you read the code. Model.kt holds the types and needs no changes.
settle: a cache hit on an already-posted payment must not fetch or post again. Rewrite it without ?: run.
capture: return the captured copy.
buildRequest: the order id belongs in request.reference, not metadata.reference.
feeLabel: show the merchant's name, not the schedule's. Use named values instead of it.
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then run the five-second checklist over your four functions.
hints: For settle, decide the payment first (cached ?: fetch()), then post it once. ?: return handles the duplicate.
capture is a two-branch if expression. It needs no scope function.
In buildRequest, a nested apply with one line inside can become metadata.channel = "ecom".
In feeLabel, two vals, each with ?: return "...", read top to bottom and can't mix up the merchant and the schedule.

drill.title: The grid from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Draw the 2x2 grid (this or it, the object or the block's result) and put the five functions in it. Then write one payments line for each, and next to it, what the whole expression evaluates to. Check your grid against the figure.

answer.html: // returns the object | returns the block's result // this: apply | run, with // it: also | let val req = PaymentRequest().apply { amount = total; merchantId = "m-42" } // the request val auth = gateway.authorize(req).also { audit.record(it) } // the authorization val risk = req.run { riskModel.score(amount, merchantId) } // the score val line = with(auth) { "$code for $amountMinor" } // the String val entry = card.token?.let { vault.lookup(it) } // the lookup result, or null

alt.html: // Java has no scope functions; each line is the plain Java it stands for PaymentRequest req = new PaymentRequest(); req.setAmount(total); req.setMerchantId("m-42"); Authorization auth = gateway.authorize(req); audit.record(auth); long risk = riskModel.score(req.getAmount(), req.getMerchantId()); String line = auth.code() + " for " + auth.amountMinor(); VaultEntry entry = card.token() == null ? null : vault.lookup(card.token());

recap: A scope function is a tiny inline function: it runs a block with the object as this (run, with, apply) or it (let, also), and returns the object (apply, also) or the block's result (let, run, with).
Pick by two questions: what should the expression give back, and does the block use the object's members or pass the object along?
All five are inline and declare callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE): no lambda objects, a val can be assigned inside, and a bare return leaves the enclosing function.
x?.let { A } ?: B runs B whenever A evaluates to null, not only when x is null. When A can be null, write if or when.
also and apply drop the block's result, and nested receivers and nested it quietly pick the innermost one. None of these gets a warning.
Nullable types replace Optional: ?. maps, ?: defaults, returns or throws, takeIf filters, and requireNotNull/checkNotNull fail with a message and smart-cast.

explain.prompt: A teammate writes repo.find(id)?.let { cache.put(id, it) } ?: run { log.warn("missing $id") } and says it means "cache it if found, warn if not". cache is a HashMap. Explain when it does something else, and what you'd write instead.
explain.answer: The Elvis operator doesn't look at what find returned. It looks at the value of the whole left side, which is the result of the let block, and that is whatever cache.put returned. HashMap.put returns the previous value for the key, which is null the first time. So every time an entity is found and cached for the first time, the block returns null and the warning runs too: "missing" gets logged for entities that were found. It only behaves as intended when an older value was already cached. I'd write the branch I mean: val entity = repo.find(id); if (entity != null) cache[id] = entity else log.warn("missing $id"). Or, since caching is only a side effect, repo.find(id)?.also { cache[id] = it } ?: log.warn(...), because also returns the entity itself, which is not null.

deeper.html:
Two things are changing around scope functions, and one tool can enforce the checklist for you.

The return-value checker. Kotlin 2.3.0 added an Experimental checker that warns when you ignore a function's result. It is off by default; -Xreturn-value-checker=check reports ignored results of functions the standard library marks, and full treats every function as marked. In Kotlin 2.4.21, all six scope functions (the five plus non-extension run) carry @IgnorableReturnValue, so payment.let { it.copy(status = CAPTURED) } as a bare statement is not reported. takeIf and takeUnless don't carry it. On the standard library's main branch, after 2.4.21, let, run and with have dropped @IgnorableReturnValue for a new returnsResultOf(block) contract, which Kotlin 2.4.0 introduced as Experimental. With it, the checker can tell x?.let { builder.append(it) } (fine to ignore) from x?.let { "kotlin.$it" } (a value you computed and dropped). Which release will ship that change isn't known yet. apply and also keep @IgnorableReturnValue, so the also { it.copy() } bug stays invisible to the checker.

Labels for nested receivers. When you can't avoid a nested receiver, this@label says which one you mean. Two nested apply blocks share the implicit label @apply, so you need your own: form.apply outer@{ fx.apply { this@outer.amount = 500 } }. If you need a label, that is usually a sign to flatten the code instead.

Detekt. Detekt 1.23.8, the current stable release, has rules for most of the checklist: UnnecessaryLet, UnnecessaryApply (active by default since 1.16.0), AlsoCouldBeApply and UseLet in the style rule set, and NestedScopeFunctions in the complexity rule set. Apart from UnnecessaryApply, they are off until you enable them. UseLet pulls the other way from UnnecessaryLet: it wants if (x != null) f(x) else null written as x?.let { f(it) }. A rule of thumb that satisfies both: use ?.let when the non-null value flows into an expression, and use if on a local val for control flow and for branches with more than one statement.
